en: (PrMoSū_Mū-LCh) Pārājika 2: Should any monk, whether in a village or in the wilderness, take what belongs to others and has not been given, which is considered theft—such that for taking what was not given, a king or a royal minister might seize him, and either kill him, bind him, or banish him, saying to him: "O man, you are a fool; you are a simpleton"—[that monk is defeated].
If a monk should take what has not been given, such as by saying "you are a thief," this monk also incurs a defeat and is no longer in communion.

Pārājika 3: Furthermore, if a monk should intentionally deprive a human being or one who has the form of a human being of life with his own hand, or should provide him with a weapon, or should seek out a weapon-bearer for him, [desiring] death;

He would incite him to death or describe the praises of death to him, and would say to him: "O man, what use have you for this wretched, impure, and miserable life? O man, death is better for you than life. With thoughts and intentions approved by such reflections, he would in many ways incite him to death or describe the praises of death to him.
And if he should die because of that, this monk also becomes one who has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pārājika 4: Should any monk, not knowing and not fully understanding, while lacking and not possessing it, claim to have attained a distinction, or knowledge, or vision, or a state of ease, saying, "I know this;
I see this," and if at a later time, whether being questioned or not, he is found to have fallen into that offense and seeks purification—[he is one who has committed a pārājika offense].
If he should say, "Venerable sirs, not knowing, I said 'I know'; not seeing, I said 'I see'... this monk also becomes one who has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.

Venerable sirs, the four *pārājika* rules have been recited by me. If a monk commits any one of these offenses, he does not obtain communal residence or shared enjoyment with the monks, neither before nor after; he becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.

In this regard, venerable sirs, I ask you: I ask a second and even a third time—Are you pure in this matter? Are you pure in this matter, venerable sirs, since there is silence? Thus it is. *Uddāna* (SA.4–13): ... wandering, sexual intercourse, a small hut, a large dwelling, groundless [accusation], malicious speech, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, following such a person, corrupting families, and abusive speech...
These, venerable sirs, are indeed the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules that come up for recitation in the *Prātimokṣasūtra* every half-month.
(PrMoSū-LCh) SA.1 Intentionally emitting semen, except during a dream, is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
(PrMoSū-LCh) SA.2 Should any monk, with a mind affected by lust, engage in physical contact with a woman, such as taking her hand or [taking] her arm...
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.33 [is a] *pāyantika*.
Having accepted two or three bowlfuls, one should go outside the monastery and share them with virtuous monks; one may also consume some oneself—this is the proper occasion for that.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.34: Should any monk, having already finished his meal and being invited to stop, eat or consume solid or soft food that has not been made *nirikta* (declared as leftover), it is a *pāyantika*.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.35: Should any monk, knowing that another monk has already finished his meal and has been invited to desist, and knowing that there is no surplus food, should excessively invite him to further food by saying, "Eat this, O Venerable One; consume this," with the intent of providing [more] and thinking, "Perhaps this monk will be provided with more," and doing so for that very reason, it is a *pāyantika*.
(Pāy. 36) Eating in a group, except on an appropriate occasion, is an offense of expiation.

In this regard, these are the exceptions: the time of illness, the time of ritual activity, the time of travel, boarding a boat, a great assembly, and a meal for ascetics; these are the exceptions in that case.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.37: Should any monk eat or consume solid or soft food at an improper time, it is an offense of expiation.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.38: Should any monk eat or consume fresh or cooked food that has been stored, there is an offense of expiation.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.39: Should any monk consume as food that which has not been given, other than water and tooth-sticks, it is an offense of expiation (pāyantikā).
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.40: Those foods which have been declared by the Blessed One to be delicacies for monks, namely: milk, curd, fresh butter, fish, meat, and dried meat.
Furthermore, if a monk, being not ill, should request for his own sake such choice foods from other families and then eat or consume them, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāyattika 41–50: Summary Verse.

In the case of consuming food containing living beings, there is a formal standing; in the case of sitting [inappropriately], being naked, or [approaching] an army, one should go for two nights as a mendicant (udyūṣika). [The offenses of] striking, threatening to strike, and grave misconduct [are also dealt with here].
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.41: Should any monk, knowing that water contains living beings, consume it, there is an offense of expiation.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.42: Should any monk, knowing that a family is engaged in a meal, sit down on a seat after intruding upon them, it is an offense of expiation.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.43: Should any monk, knowing that a family is engaged in a meal, remain standing in a secluded and concealed place, it is an offense of expiation.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.44: Should any monk give hard or soft food to a naked ascetic, or to a female naked ascetic, or to a wandering mendicant, or to a female wandering mendicant, at sunset, it is an offense of expiation.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.45: Should any monk go to see an army that has been mobilized, it is an offense of expiation.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.46: Should a monk have such a reason as to go and see an army that is mobilized, that monk may stay apart from that army for at most two nights. If he should stay apart longer than that, it is an offense of expiation (pāyantika).

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.47: If a monk, while staying apart from his community for even two nights within that army, should go to the front of the battle, or to the tip of the banner, or to the vanguard of the force, or should witness the array of the army or the display of its divisions, it is a *pāyattika*.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.48: Should any monk, being resentful, angry, fierce, and displeased, give a blow to another monk, it is an offense of expiation.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.49: Should any monk, being resentful, angry, fierce, and displeased, raise his hand to strike another monk—even if only with the palm of his hand—it is a *pāyattika*.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.50: Should any monk, knowing of a fellow monk’s grave offense, conceal it, there is an offense of expiation.
The summary verse: Contact, light, meter, not conferring full ordination, one who speaks according to the Dharma, a novice monk, disfigurement, and the time of the burning of the jewels.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.51: Should any monk say to another monk, "Come, venerable one, let us go to the families; there I will have you given excellent food, both hard and soft, as much as you desire," and having failed to have it given to him, he should afterwards say, "Go away, venerable one, I have no pleasure in conversation with you. This is an offense of expiation.

Or whether it be while walking or sitting, if a certain monk— observing his opportunity for provocation and thinking, "This monk will surely be provoked by me during conversation or while sitting"— does so solely with the intention of provoking him, there is an offense of expiation (pāyantika).
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.52: Should any monk, not being ill, for his own sake, kindle a fire or cause one to be kindled with the intention of warming himself, it is an offense of expiation.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.53: Should any monk, having given his consent for a legitimate business of the Saṃgha, subsequently become resentful, angry, fierce, displeased, and commit an act of reviling, saying, "Give back your consent, monk! I will not give it to you," there is an offense of expiation (pāyantikā).
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.54: Should any monk, together with a person who has not received full ordination, lie down in the same dwelling for more than two nights, it is an offense of expiation.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.55: Should any monk speak thus: "As I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, those things called 'obstructive states' by the Blessed One are not sufficient to constitute an obstruction when they are indulged in," that monk should be addressed by the other monks as follows: "Venerable sir, do not speak thus: 'As I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One...'"

"I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One such that those things called obstructive factors by the Blessed One are not actually capable of being obstacles when practiced. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not right to misrepresent the Blessed One; yet the Blessed One has not said this. On the contrary, venerable sir, in many ways the Blessed One has stated that obstructive factors are indeed obstructive.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One, and those [practices], when indulged in, are sufficient for being obstacles.

"Venerable one, relinquish this kind of evil view. If that monk, being thus addressed by the monks, relinquishes that matter, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, he should be examined and instructed a second and a third time for the sake of relinquishing that matter. A second and a third time...
If, being questioned and instructed up to three times, he should relinquish that matter, that is well;
if he does not relinquish it, there is an offense of expiation (pāyantika).

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.56: Should any monk, knowing that a person speaks in such a manner, has not acted in accordance with the Dharma, and has not relinquished that evil view, converse with him, talk with him, live together with him, eat together with him,
or share a dwelling or sleep under the same roof with him, it is an offense of expiation.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.57 If a novice (śramaṇoddeśa) should speak thus: "As I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, those sensual pleasures which have been declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive are not, when indulged in, sufficient to constitute an obstruction," that novice should be addressed by the monks as follows: "Do not, venerable novice, speak thus."

"I speak thus because I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that those sensual pleasures which have been declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive are not sufficient to constitute an obstruction when indulged in. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is not right to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One has not said such a thing. On the contrary, in many ways he has stated that sensual pleasures are indeed obstructive."

"The Blessed One has declared that these are indeed obstructive things, and that when practiced, they are sufficient to constitute an obstruction. Therefore, O Venerable Śrāmaṇeraka, relinquish this evil view. If, being thus addressed by the monks, that śrāmaṇeraka relinquishes that matter, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, [the formal procedure must be carried out].
He should be exhorted and instructed a second and even a third time for the relinquishing of that matter.

If, being exhorted and instructed a second and even a third time, he should relinquish that matter, that would be well; but if he does not relinquish it, that novice (śramaṇoddeśa) should be addressed by the monks as follows: "From this day forward..."

"Venerable one, O *śramaṇoddeśa*, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, is not to be designated as your teacher; nor should any other wise fellow-celibate who occupies the position of a guru be followed closely behind you. Furthermore, other *śramaṇoddeśas* receive even a moment’s [instruction] from this monk."
Thinking, "It will not be touched," and making this very the reason, it is a *pāyantika*.
"They obtain, together with the monks, shared lodging and sleeping for up to two nights; even that is no longer yours from this day forward. Go away, you deluded man, perish!"

Furthermore, if a monk, knowing that a novice has not yet been properly trained, should admit him into the community, support him, or share a dwelling with him under the same roof, it is an offense of expiation (pāyantika).
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.58: If a monk, upon obtaining a robe, does not take up one or another of the three means for discolouring it—

namely, blue, mud-coloured, or madder-red— and should a monk, without having taken up one or another of these three means for discolouring it— blue, mud-coloured, or madder-red— use a new robe, there is an offense of expiation (pāyantika).

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.59: Should any monk, with his own hand, pick up or cause to be picked up a jewel or what is considered a jewel, except when it is within a monastery or within a dwelling, there is an offense of expiation.
If a monk, while staying in a monastery garden or a dwelling, [acts as follows]...
[text missing] ...
Pāyantika 63: For poking with a finger, there is an offense of expiation.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.64. There is an offense entailing expiation for splashing about in water.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.65: Should any monk lie down in the same dwelling with a woman, it is an offense of expiation.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.66: Should any monk frighten another monk, or cause him to be frightened—even if only as a joke—it is an offense of expiation (pāyantikā).

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.67: Should any monk, however, hide or cause to be hidden the bowl, robe, shoulder-bag, water-strainer, waist-band, or any other requisite for the livelihood of a monk, nun, female trainee, male novice, or female novice—
unless there is a specific reason for doing so— he commits a *pāyattika*.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.68: Should any monk, having given a robe to another monk, subsequently use it without having it returned, there is an offense of expiation (pāyantikā).

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.69: Should any monk, out of malice and with a mind of hatred, being dissatisfied, falsely accuse a pure monk who has not committed an offense by means of a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rule, it is a *pāyattika*.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.70: Should any monk travel along a road together with a woman who is not accompanied by a man, even as far as the next village, it is a *pāyattika*.
The summary verse: Theft, the twenty, digging, the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), training, quarrels, departing in silence, out of disrespect, drinking intoxicants, and [eating] at the improper time.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.71: Should any monk travel along a highway together with a caravan of thieves, even if only as far as another village, it is an offense of expiation (pāyantika).
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.72: Should any monk ordain a person who is less than twenty years of age for the state of a monk, it is an offense of expiation.
That person is not fully ordained, and those monks are to be censured; this is the rule in that case.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.73: Should any monk dig the earth with his own hand, or cause it to be dug, there is an offense of expiation.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.74: A monk must accept the invitation for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony every four months, except at the proper time; [otherwise, it is] a *pāyantika*.
In this regard, the exception is as follows: an individual invitation, repeated invitations, an excessive invitation, and a permanent invitation; this is the exception in that case.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.75: Should any monk, when being addressed by other monks, saying, "Venerable sir, you ought to train yourself in the training," speak thus: "I will not train myself in this training according to the word of you who are foolish, deluded, unskilled, and incompetent, until I have questioned other monks who are bearers of the Sūtras, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātṛkās," there is an offense of expiation (pāyantika).

A monk who desires to understand should train in that training and consult monks who are masters of the Sūtras, masters of the Vinaya, and masters of the Mātṛkās; this is the proper occasion for doing so.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy 76: Should any monk, while monks are living in quarrel, strife, contention, and dispute, stand by in silence as an eavesdropper, thinking, "What these monks say,
having heard that, I shall report accordingly"— if he does so for this very reason, it is an offense of expiation (pāyantika).

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.77: Should any monk, while a formal legal discourse concerning the Dharma is being delivered by the Saṅgha, depart in silence without having informed a monk who is present—unless there is a specific reason for doing so—he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
(Pāy. 78) An offense of expiation for disrespect.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy. 79: For drinking fermented liquor, distilled spirits, or intoxicants, there is an offense of expiation.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy. 80: Should any monk enter a village at an improper time without having looked back at a monk who is present, except when there is a specific reason for doing so, it is an offense of expiation. // Ṛ //
The summary verse: Regarding eating together, dawn, giving, needles, needle-cases, and foot-rests; binding, sitting mats, itching, shawls, and the robe of the Sugata. // Ṛ //

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.81: Should any monk, having been invited to a family where a meal is being served, go among families for alms before the meal or after the meal, without first informing a householder who is present—unless there is a specific reason for doing so—he commits a *pāyattika*.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pāy.82: Should any monk, when the night has not yet ended, before the dawn has risen, and while the jewels or what are considered as jewels have not yet been removed, enter the royal palace of an anointed Kṣatriya king, or its precincts, [beyond the threshold]... [incurs a pāyattika].
The Venerable Ones are pure in this matter, since they are silent; thus do I understand it.

The summary verse: Regarding the village and the interior of the house, the training rules for forest-dwellers, and the offenses requiring confession—these have been proclaimed by the Buddha, the speaker of what is beneficial.
Furthermore, venerable ones, these four *pratideśanīya* dharmas come up for recitation every half-month in the *Prātimokṣasūtra*.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Pratid.1: Whatever monk, having received with his own hand hard food or soft food from an unrelated nun who has come onto the street while wandering for alms in a village, should eat or consume it, he must confess it.

Having gone outside the monastery, the monk must confess it in the presence of the other monks: "Venerable sirs, I have fallen into a blameworthy state that is unseemly and requires confession; I confess that offense. This offense is one that requires confession."
(Pratid.2) If many monks are invited to a family for a meal,
and a nun stands there directing them, saying, "Give solid food here, give rice here, give soup here,
give more here," that nun should be addressed by those monks as follows: "Please wait a moment."

"Sister, remain silent for a moment while these monks are eating. Even if it does not occur to a single monk to speak thus to the nun, all those monks should say: 'Venerable ones, we have committed a censurable act; we have fallen into an unseemly state and must go outside the monastery to confess it before the monks.'"
We confess this offense which requires confession; this offense, too, is one that requires confession. (Pratid.
3) Those families which belong to the Saṃgha as families subject to training and which have been designated as being under the restraint of training—

Furthermore, if a monk, having previously been uninvited, approaches families that are under training by the Saṅgha and are recognized as being subject to the discipline of training, and there, having taken hard or soft food with his own hand, eats or consumes it,
that monk must go outside the monastery and confess before the monks: "I am blameworthy."
Venerable sirs, I have fallen into a situation that is improper and requires confession; I confess that offense. This offense, too, is one requiring confession (Pratid.4):
those lodgings belonging to the Saṅgha which are in the wilderness, regarded as suspicious, regarded as dangerous, and regarded as fearful and terrifying.

Furthermore, if a monk, having accepted solid or soft food in a forest dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha that is of such a nature as to be considered suspicious, dangerous, or terrifying, and which is entirely unannounced within the forest, and then eats or consumes it at the edge of the monastery grounds, that monk must confess it before the other monks.
"Venerable sirs, I have fallen into a censurable and unwholesome state that requires confession; I confess that offense.
This offense, too, is one that requires confession."
Venerable sirs, the four *pratideśanīya* dharmas have been recited by me. Regarding this, I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this matter? A second time and a third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
Since there is silence, the venerable ones are pure in this regard; thus do I understand it to be.
Summary verse: There are seven [offenses] regarding the lower robe, three regarding the upper robe, and [those involving] being covered, veiled, or leaping with the body.
Venerable ones, these many rules for those in training indeed come up for recitation in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half-month.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Śai.1 One should train oneself thus: "I shall put on the lower robe in a circular shape."

(PrMoSū-LCh) Śai.2–7: "We shall put on the lower robe neither too high nor too low, not like an elephant’s trunk, not like a palm fan, not like a lump of boiled beans, and not like an elephant’s head"—this training is to be observed.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Śai.8: "We shall wear the robe in a rounded manner"—this training is to be observed.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Śai.9–10: "We shall wear the robe neither too high nor too low"—this training is to be observed.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Śaikṣa 11–15: "We shall go among the houses well-restrained, well-covered, making little noise, with eyes cast down, looking only a yoke’s length ahead"—this training is to be observed.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Śai.16–20: “We shall not go among the houses with our heads covered, nor with our robes pulled over one shoulder, nor with our robes tucked up, nor with our arms akimbo, nor with our robes wrapped around the neck”—this training is to be observed.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Śai.21–25: “We shall not go among the houses with our robes hitched up, nor with them tucked under the armpits, nor squatting on our heels, nor with our bodies bent forward while squatting, nor with hands on our hips”—this training is to be observed.

(PrMoSū-LCh) Śai.26–30: “We shall not go among the houses shaking the body, nor shaking the arms, nor shaking the head, nor with shoulders hunched, nor with hands clasped together”—this training is to be observed.
One should compose a summary: "I shall not sit down," as well as the eight [rules] regarding receiving, the five, four, seven, and five [rules] concerning eating with respect and so forth.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Śai.31 One should train oneself thus: "I shall not sit on a seat inside a house without having been invited."

(PrMoSū-LCh) Śaikṣa 32–39: One should train oneself thus: "I will not sit on a seat within a house without first inspecting it; nor with the whole body collapsed; nor placing one foot upon the other; nor placing one ankle upon the other; nor placing one thigh upon the other; nor with feet drawn together; nor with feet spread apart; nor in a cross-legged posture. This is the training to be observed.
(PrMoSū-LCh) Śai.40 One should train oneself thus: "We shall receive almsfood with due respect."

(PrMoSū-LCh) Śai.41–43: “We shall receive almsfood with the bowl held level, with an equal amount of curry, and with distinct portions, while maintaining the perception that it is in the bowl”—this training is to be observed.
